newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: UNHCR says 50,000 leave Kabul since Taleban arrive.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR says 50,000 leave Kabul since Taleban arrive.

text.p: Up to 50,000 people have left Kabul since the radical Taleban militia captured the city in late September, according to figures from the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

The figures, which were collected at a UNHCR checkpoint on the road leading east from Kabul towards the Pakistani border, showed that 49,099 people left Kabul and 8,631 returned in the period from October 1 to December 7.
"People are uncertain about their future in Kabul. The economy is continuing to deteriorate and unemployment is rising," Terry Pitzner, head of the UNHCR in Kabul, said on Wednesday.

The exodus peaked in early November, when more than 6,300 people left Kabul in a single week. Over recent weeks the number of returnees has risen, although there is still a net exodus of over 3,000 people a week.
The most common destinations for refugees are Pakistan, where many Afghans displaced in the 1980s during the Soviet occupation of their country still reside, and the eastern Afghan city of Jalalabad.
Jalalabad has huge refugee camps dating from the time when Kabul was the front line between the factions in Afghanistan's four-year-old civil war.
The Taleban who control more than two thirds of the country are currently battling against the forces of the ousted government and a powerful northern leader.

"Approximately 1.4 million refugees remain in Iran and, close to 900,000 in Pakistan. As fighting continues in some areas of the country, people continue to move, and this trend is likely to persist," a recently released appeal document said.
"An estimated one million internally displaced persons are living away from their homes," the document said.
The international community launched a consolidated U.N. coordinated appeal on December 3 aiming to raise $133 million in aid for Afghanistan during 1997.
